text: A rock slide on the main line east of Yale at four o'clock on the morning of November 3, 1906, buried the track to a depth of thirty feet for a distance of 200 yards. The westbound express was held at North Bend while extra gangs worked by lantern light to clear it. No one was hurt. The slide came from a cut that had been giving trouble since the autumn rains began, and the roadmaster had posted a watchman at the spot only the week before. It was he who flagged the eastbound freight with his lantern a few minutes after the rock came down. Engineers say more loose rock hangs above the track.

text: PAKENHAM, Ont., April 27, 1909. — About ten acres of farmland on the clay bank of the Mississippi River slid into the stream early on Sunday, carrying away a barn, a stable and a quantity of fencing. The farmer and his family had left the house half an hour before to attend church. The river was dammed for some hours and backed up over the flats. Old residents say the bank had been cracking since the thaw. A gang of men with teams was put to work cutting a channel through the clay.
label: ground

text: Two miners were swept to their deaths by a snowslide that struck the upper workings of a silver mine above Sandon, B.C., on February 2, 1911. Their bodies were recovered after two days of digging. The slide followed a week of heavy snow and a sudden rise in temperature. The slide also carried away the upper terminal of the aerial tramway, and the mine will be closed for some weeks. The manager says the bunkhouses had been moved last year away from the old slide path, but that this slide came down a gully where none had been seen in living memory. Miners in the camp have petitioned the company for a snowshed over the trail to the workings.

text: Earthquake. A sharp shock was felt at Ottawa and through the Upper Ottawa valley at 9:17 o'clock last night, December 8, 1922. Dishes rattled from shelves, and in Pembroke the bell of one church was set ringing. No serious damage is reported. In Arnprior a woman fainted, and at a lumber camp up the river men rushed from the bunkhouse believing a boiler had exploded. Observers at the Dominion Observatory said the shock was centred some distance up the valley.
label: ground

text: Mud slide on the Grand Trunk Pacific east of Prince Rupert, November 1913; line blocked two days.
label: ground

text: STEWART, B.C., March 14, 1915. — A snowslide of enormous size came down the mountain behind the mine camp at half past two this morning and carried the bunkhouse, the cookhouse and the blacksmith shop into the gulch below. Of the twenty-two men asleep in the bunkhouse, fourteen were dug out alive, several of them badly injured; eight are dead. The rescuers worked through the night in snow forty feet deep, guided by the cries of the buried men. Snow has fallen almost without pause for nine days, and the slide paths on both sides of the valley are loaded. The company has ordered all work suspended until the danger is past.
label: ground

text: An earthquake was felt in Victoria and along the east coast of Vancouver Island on the afternoon of June 9, 1926. Chimneys were cracked in a number of houses at Courtenay and goods were thrown from the shelves of stores. A series of lighter shocks followed during the night. At Comox the water in the harbour was seen to rise and fall several feet in a few minutes, and a number of small boats broke from their moorings. Residents of the Cowichan valley reported a loud rumbling, and at one logging camp a section of hillside slid onto the railway grade. Many people remained outdoors until long after midnight.

text: A great slide of muck and gravel came down the hillside above Bonanza Creek on the morning of July 2, 1908, overwhelming two cabins and a dredge camp. One man was killed. The slope had been undermined by thawing ground and by hydraulic mining. Miners on the claims below have been warned to move their camps.
label: ground

text: Brule, Alta., May 1916: rock slide closes the coal road; tipple workers escape uninjured.
label: ground

text: The river bank slumped into the Red River south of the city on the night of April 30, 1923, carrying away part of a market garden and leaving a house on the edge of a fresh cliff twenty feet high. The city engineer has ordered the family out. Engineers say other homes along that stretch may also be in danger.
label: ground

text: A sinkhole forty feet across and of unknown depth opened suddenly in a pasture near Windsor, N.S., on the morning of August 8, 1905. A cow grazing nearby fell into it and was not recovered. The ground in that district rests on gypsum, and the old people say such holes have opened before. Hundreds of people drove out from the town on Sunday to view the hole, which had partly filled with water by evening. A farmer from the district told the reporter that his father had lost a horse in a similar pit many years ago. The government geologist has been asked to examine the ground, and the owner has put up a rail fence to keep the curious away from the edge.
label: ground

text: PETTY HARBOUR, Nfld., February 1924. — A snowslide came down the steep hill at the back of the harbour after the blizzard on Monday and struck two dwelling-houses. A mother and her child were killed; four others were taken out alive. The men of the harbour dug with shovels and their bare hands for three hours. The houses stood under a cliff where the drifting snow had piled high during the storm.
label: ground

text: MURRAY BAY, Que., September 1931. A smart earthquake shock was felt here and along the north shore of the river at about 11 o'clock Tuesday night. Summer cottagers still in residence were roused from their beds, plaster fell in several houses and a stone chimney collapsed at the hotel. There were two lighter tremors before dawn. The shock lasted perhaps ten seconds, and many said it was preceded by a low rumble like distant thunder. Telephone communication with the upper villages was interrupted for several hours. Old residents say the district is subject to such shocks, but no one could remember the bells in the parish church ringing by themselves before.
label: ground

text: Rock fall, Thompson canyon, October 1927. A mass of loose rock dislodged by autumn rains came down onto the railway two miles above Spences Bridge, striking the locomotive of a freight train and pushing it to the edge of the river. The engineer and fireman jumped clear. The line was closed for eighteen hours. Crews used dynamite to break up the larger boulders. The railway has since strung a slide-detector fence along the cut, which will set the signals at danger if rock strikes the wires.
label: ground

text: The clay bank behind the village of Gatineau Point gave way during the spring thaw of 1904, carrying three small houses down to the water's edge. Their occupants had been warned the day before by cracks in the ground and escaped. The slide left a raw scar about 300 feet long.
label: ground

text: A mud slide caused by heavy rains swept down a gully on the North Shore mountains on November 19, 1919, and buried a logging road and two cabins under six feet of mud and boulders. A logger was killed. Rain had fallen almost without stop for eleven days. The road was closed for a week while crews cleared it.
label: ground

text: White Pass railway, March 1920: avalanche buries section house near the summit; section foreman and wife rescued after six hours.
label: ground

text: Earthquake felt Montreal, 3:50 p.m., May 22, 1909. Brief tremor; office buildings swayed on St. James Street; no damage.

text: For several weeks in the spring of 1912 the farmers along the Rivière du Nord near Lachute watched a long crack widen in the field above the river. On the morning of May 6 the whole slope let go at once. Some 25 acres of clay flowed into the valley like porridge in a matter of minutes, burying the road and a house. The family of seven had moved out only the night before. A dam of mud blocked the river and the water rose behind it until it cut a new channel two days later.
label: ground

text: Rock and earth slid across the road and the railway near Field on August 11, 1932, after a cloudburst on the slopes above. Traffic was held for a day.
label: ground

text: VICTORIA, Dec. 1951. An earthquake of considerable force, centred somewhere off the west coast of Vancouver Island, rocked the city at 4:23 this morning. Many people ran into the streets in their nightclothes. Windows were broken downtown and several chimneys toppled in Oak Bay. Seismologists at the observatory said it was the strongest shock recorded there in some years. A wharf at a west-coast cannery village was reported damaged by an unusual rise and fall of the tide shortly after the shock, and a lighthouse keeper reported rock falls from the cliffs near his station. Telephone lines up-island were down for several hours. Three aftershocks were felt before daylight.
label: ground

text: A rock slide closed the Trans-Canada Highway in the Fraser Canyon just north of Boston Bar on the night of January 20, 1959. A truck driver was killed when a boulder the size of a house struck his cab. Highways crews said freezing and thawing had loosened the rock face. The highway was reopened to one-lane traffic after 36 hours.
label: ground

text: A landslide in the soft clay of the Ottawa River bank west of Rockland carried away a farmhouse, a barn, and some 600 feet of the county road on May 3, 1962. The occupants escaped after hearing loud cracking noises during the night. Geologists said the clay had been saturated by melting snow and spring rain. The slide, which occurred shortly before dawn, left a crescent-shaped scar about 1,200 feet across and sent a tongue of liquefied clay well out into the river, where it formed a mudbank that will have to be dredged to keep the channel open. Residents of two other farms nearby were asked to leave until engineers could examine the bank.
label: ground

text: Avalanche control crews on the Salmo-Creston highway at Kootenay Pass triggered a slide on February 18, 1971, that buried the road under snow 25 feet deep. Nobody was caught. The highway was closed for 30 hours while rotary plows cleared it. It was one of the largest slides ever recorded on that road.
label: ground

text: Two skiers were killed and a third was rescued alive by a probe line after an avalanche swept a slope outside the boundary of a ski area near Banff on March 2, 1969. Wardens said a wind slab had built up on the slope after several days of strong winds. The three men, all experienced skiers from Calgary, had been warned at the hill that the out-of-bounds slopes were closed. The survivor was buried under about four feet of snow for nearly an hour and was taken to hospital in Banff suffering from exposure. Park officials said they would review the signs at the area boundary.
label: ground

text: A local tsunami was generated in a remote inlet north of Bella Coola in October 1968 when an estimated two million cubic metres of rock fell from a cliff into the water. The wave stripped trees from the shoreline to a height of 40 metres opposite the slide and swamped a logging camp float six kilometres away. Two men at the camp were injured. The slide was not witnessed. Geologists who visited the site the following summer found that the cliff had been undercut by a retreating glacier and fractured by seasonal freezing and thawing.
label: ground

text: A sinkhole about 30 feet across opened in a wheat field near Esterhazy, Sask., in August 1957, swallowing a part of a farmer's grain crop. Geologists said salt beds deep beneath the area may have been dissolved by groundwater. The farmer said there was no warning.
label: ground

text: TIMMINS, Ont., 1964. Subsidence over old mine workings has caused several houses on a street in the south end to tilt, crack and settle as much as two feet. Residents have been asked to leave until the ground is surveyed. The mining company is paying for temporary accommodation.
label: ground

text: Earthquake, Yukon, 1972: magnitude 6.0 shock felt at Whitehorse and Haines Junction; some cracked walls and fallen goods, rock falls on the Alaska Highway.
label: ground

text: A landslide in the Peace River valley near Dunvegan in May 1957 dammed a tributary creek for several days. Farmland upstream was flooded until the water breached the debris.

text: Mud slides caused by torrential rains blocked the highway between Penticton and Summerland on June 12, 1948, and several orchards were partially buried. A woman was injured when mud broke through the back wall of her house. Several orchardists lost young trees. Road crews worked through the night with shovels and a grader to reopen a single lane, and the trains were held at Summerland.
label: ground

text: Rock fall, Petty Harbour, Nfld., October 1953: boulders crash down the cliff onto two houses; one man injured.
label: ground

text: A landslide estimated at four million cubic yards fell from the side of a valley in the northern Rockies in the spring of 1960 and blocked a river. The new lake behind the slide drowned a trapper's cabin and part of a winter road, and RCMP flew in to warn people downstream in case the natural dam failed. It held, and the river cut a channel over it within a month. Geologists who flew over the site said the slope had been weakened by the spring thaw.
label: ground

text: A heavy snowfall followed by a quick warming triggered dozens of avalanches in Rogers Pass in January 1967. One of them struck a stalled car on the Trans-Canada Highway, killing the driver. The highway was closed for three days while avalanche crews brought down the remaining loaded slopes with artillery. More than a metre of new snow had fallen in four days, followed by rain at lower elevations, and avalanche crews said the snowpack was among the most unstable they had seen since the highway opened. Hundreds of motorists were stranded at Revelstoke and Golden, filling every motel room, while trucks were lined up for miles on both approaches to the pass.
label: ground

text: A small clay slide near Lachute, Que., in April 1958 carried away a barn and two cows.

text: Earth tremor shakes Toronto. A shock originating south of Lake Ontario was felt across the city at 8:12 p.m. on August 13, 1967, rattling windows and swaying the upper floors of office towers. No damage was reported. Hundreds of people telephoned the newspapers and the police to ask whether a gas main had exploded.

text: The rockfall that struck a car on the Squamish highway on the evening of April 4, 1964, killed two people. Rain had been falling heavily for two days.

text: A snow avalanche crushed the bunkhouse at a mine near Stewart in January 1955; two men killed.

text: A magnitude 4.8 earthquake struck about 15 km northwest of Shawville, Que., at 03:42 local time on February 23, 1999. It was felt across eastern Ontario and western Quebec, including Ottawa, Montreal and Kingston. Minor damage was reported in the epicentral area: cracked plaster, broken dishes and a few fallen chimneys. No injuries. Several aftershocks were recorded over the following week.

text: Landslide, Prince George, 2000: slope failure along the Nechako River cutbank forced residents of six homes to evacuate. Geotechnical engineers said the clay bank had been destabilized by a wet spring and erosion at its toe. The homes were later condemned.
